# Letter of Jeremiah Chapter 1 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Vaticanus, Letter of Jeremiah 1
**Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/LJR_001_page_001.jpg

---

## Council Decision

The Letter of Jeremiah is sustained satirical polemic — a rhetorical tour de force in which vivid ridicule of idol worship builds relentlessly to its recurring refrain. The council agrees that the translation must preserve the satirical bite while remaining accessible. PNEUMA's energy is adopted as the base register; EMET's structural precision informs several key passages; LOGOS provides the connective tissue of clarity. The repeating refrain is standardized as: **"From this it is evident that they are not gods; do not fear them."**

---

**1** This is a copy of the letter that Jeremiah sent to the exiles being taken captive to Babylon by the Babylonian king — a message he was commanded by God to deliver.

**2** Because of the sins you have committed against God, you will be taken to Babylon as captives by Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians.

**3** Once you arrive in Babylon, you will remain there many years, for a long time — as long as seven generations. After that I will bring you out from there in peace.

**4** In Babylon you will see gods of silver, gold, and wood being carried on people's shoulders, striking dread into the nations.

**5** Take care therefore that you do not become like the foreigners and be overcome by fear of those gods

**6** when you see the crowds pressing in from every direction, worshiping them. Say in your own hearts: "You alone, O Lord, deserve our worship."

**7** For my messenger is with you, and he himself is the guardian of your lives.

**8** Their tongues have been smoothed by the craftsman. They are plated in gold and silver. Yet they are frauds — they cannot speak.

**9** They are like a young woman fond of adornment, who fashions a crown of gold to set upon the head of her idol —

**10** while the priests take the gold away from their gods and spend it on themselves, giving some of it to the prostitutes on the rooftop.

**11** They clothe these gods of silver and gold and wood with garments, as one would dress a human being —

**12** though those gods cannot save themselves from rust and moth. Having draped them in purple robes,

**13** the priests then wipe the dust from their faces — dust that lies thick in the temple.

**14** One is held up like a governor wielding a scepter, as though he presides over wrongdoers in the land —

**15** yet he cannot bring a single sinner to justice. He holds a sword and an axe in his hand, yet he cannot deliver himself from war or thieves.

**16** From this it is evident that they are not gods; do not fear them.

**17** Just as a clay vessel becomes worthless when it breaks, so too are their gods. When set up inside houses, their eyes fill with dust from the feet of those who enter.

**18** Just as courthouse gates are locked against a criminal condemned to death, so the priests bolt their temple doors with locks and bars, lest they be plundered by robbers.

**19** Lamps are lit before them — more than are lit for themselves — yet the gods cannot see a single one.

**20** They are like one of the wooden beams in the temple. The story goes that their hearts are consumed by things that crawl from the earth; while such creatures devour them and their garments, the gods feel nothing.

**21** Their faces are blackened by the smoke that fills the house.

**22** Bats and swallows and birds come to rest on their bodies and their heads; cats do the same.

**23** From this you will know that they are not gods; do not fear them.

**24** The gold that covers them for beauty — unless someone wipes away the tarnish, it will not shine; and they felt nothing even when they were being cast.

**25** They were purchased at great price. Yet there is no breath in them.

**26** Having no feet, they are carried on shoulders, publicly displaying their own shame. And those who serve them are ashamed along with them.

**27** If one falls to the ground, it cannot rise on its own; if someone props it up, it cannot stand on its own. Offerings set before them are set before the dead.

**28** The priests sell the sacrificial offerings and pocket the proceeds; their wives cure some of the meat for themselves; but to the poor and the helpless they give nothing.

**29** Women who are ritually unclean, even women who are menstruating, handle their sacrifices. Knowing from all this that they are not gods, do not fear them.

**30** For how is it right to call these things gods? Women set the offerings before gods of silver, gold, and wood.

**31** In their temples the priests sit with garments torn, with heads and beards shaved, and with heads uncovered.

**32** They wail and cry before their gods the way people do at a funeral feast.

**33** The priests strip the robes off the gods and dress their own wives and children in them.

**34** Whether one does them harm or good, they cannot repay it. They cannot install a king or remove one.

**35** Likewise they can give neither wealth nor money. If someone makes a vow to them and fails to keep it, they will not call him to account.

**36** They cannot rescue a man from death or deliver the weak from the powerful.

**37** They cannot give sight back to a blind man; they cannot rescue a person in desperate need.

**38** They will show no mercy to the widow; they will do no good for the orphan.

**39** Their gods of wood and stone and gold and silver are like rocks on a mountain. Those who worship them will be put to shame.

**40** How then is it fitting to suppose or to say that they are gods?

**41** Even the Chaldeans themselves show no real respect for them; for when they hear of a mute man who cannot speak, they bring Bel and ask him to speak for the man, as though Bel could perceive.

**42** And yet they themselves cannot arrive at the truth and abandon these gods, for they have no capacity for understanding.

**43** Women with cords tied around them sit along the roads, burning stalks of grain.

**44** And whenever one of them is drawn aside by a passerby and lies with him, she mocks the woman next to her, sneering that she was found worthy while that one was not, and that her cord was not broken.

**45** Everything connected with these gods is a lie; how then is it fitting to suppose or say that they are gods?

**46** They are manufactured by carpenters and goldsmiths. They will be nothing other than whatever the craftsmen decide to make.

**47** And those craftsmen who made them will not themselves live long; how then can the things they made be gods?

**48** They have left only falsehood and reproach to those who come after them.

**49** For when war or catastrophe strikes, the priests consult among themselves where to go — taking their gods into hiding with them.

**50** How then can anyone fail to see that these are not gods — things that cannot save themselves from war or catastrophe?

**51** Since they are made of wood overlaid with gold and silver, it will eventually be known that they are frauds. To all nations and all kings it will be made plain: they are not gods but works of human hands, with no work of God in them.

**52** Who can be left in any doubt that they are not gods, but works of human hands, with no work of God in them?

**53** They cannot raise up a king over a land or send rain upon the people.

**54** They cannot adjudicate a case or free a land from injustice, for they are powerless — like crows that flap between heaven and earth.

**55** For when fire breaks out in a temple housing these wooden, silver, or golden gods, the priests run and save themselves, while the gods burn in the middle like beams.

**56** They cannot withstand a king or an army. How then can it be acknowledged that they are gods?

**57** Gods of wood, stone, gold, and silver cannot protect themselves from thieves and robbers.

**58** The strong will strip away their gold and silver and garments and walk off, and the gods will be helpless to stop them.

**59** Better therefore is a righteous king than a false god; better also is a household vessel that serves its owner than false gods.

**60** Better are the doors of a house that guard what is inside; better even is a wooden pillar in a palace.

**61** For the sun and the moon and the stars blaze brightly, sent out for useful purposes — they obey.

**62** Likewise the lightning, when it flashes, is visible; and wind blows throughout every land.

**63** And clouds, when God sends them over all the earth, do as they are told; and fire sent down from above to consume mountains and forests carries out its commission.

**64** But none of the idols can be compared to any one of these, either in form or in power.

**65** From which it follows that they are not to be thought or called gods — beings unable either to render judgment or to do good for people.

**66** Knowing therefore that they are not gods, do not fear them.

**67** They cannot curse kings; they cannot bless them.

**68** They show no signs in the heavens to the nations; they do not shine like the sun, nor give light like the moon.

**69** Wild animals are better than they, since animals can flee to shelter and help themselves.

**70** Therefore it is in no way clear to us that they are gods; do not fear them.

**71** For just as a scarecrow in a cucumber field protects nothing, so are their gods of wood, gold, and silver.

**72** Similarly, their gods of gold and silver and wood are like a wild-thorn in a garden on which every bird perches; or like a corpse thrown out into darkness.

**73** By the purple and linen rotting upon them you will know that they are not gods; and in the end they will be consumed and will become a reproach throughout the land.

**74** Better therefore is a righteous man who owns no idols — for he will never have to bear that reproach.
